summary.text: Quantum technology is engineering that builds devices from the laws of quantum mechanics, such as quantum sensors and quantum computers.
Governments and companies fund it heavily: the EU launched a €1 billion flagship in 2016, and a 2018 US law provides US$1 billion a year.
Its main branches are secure communication, computing, simulation and very precise sensing.

facts.label: US funding
facts.value: The 2018 National Quantum Initiative Act gives US$1 billion a year

facts.label: The qubit
facts.value: A two-level system that can be 1, 0, or a superposition

facts.label: Simulator idea
facts.value: First published by Richard Feynman in 1982

facts.label: Sensor uses
facts.value: Positioning, gravimetry, field sensing and medical diagnosis

items.prompt: A spy wants a spare copy of a qubit to read later without disturbing the original. Why does this plan fail?

options.label: Qubits are far too small for any device to detect
Measuring a quantum system changes it, so a qubit cannot be copied
Copies can be made but they decay within a day
Only government labs are legally allowed to copy them

items.explain: Measuring the properties of a quantum system causes the system to change, which is why a qubit cannot be copied.

items.prompt: Two offices share a key using entangled light, and a third party taps the line. What do the offices notice?

options.label: The message arrives faster than normal
Nothing, because quantum signals cannot be tapped silently
The interception is obvious to them
The key automatically changes to a longer one

items.explain: Quantum key distribution transmits information so that any interception of it is obvious to the users.

items.prompt: Why might a lottery prefer a quantum random number generator to an ordinary program?

options.label: It yields truly random numbers, while ordinary algorithms only imitate randomness
It produces numbers much faster than any ordinary program
It picks numbers that are more likely to win
It needs no electricity to run at all

items.explain: Non-quantum algorithms imitate randomness, while a quantum generator can produce truly random numbers.

items.prompt: A team wants to squeeze more into each use of a channel, with one qubit doing the work of two ordinary bits. Which technique is that?

options.label: Quantum teleportation
Quantum sensing
Quantum clustering
Quantum dense coding

items.explain: Dense coding uses one qubit in place of two classical bits, boosting channel capacity through entanglement.

items.prompt: Why is a machine built just to imitate one chemical compound easier to build than a general-purpose quantum computer?

options.label: It needs far fewer people to design it
It does not need complete control over every component
It works at ordinary room conditions without care
It stores information in ordinary bits only

items.explain: Quantum simulators are simpler because complete control over every component is not necessary.

items.prompt: Alice teleports a qubit's condition to Bob, far away. What actually travels to him?

options.label: The original particle, sped up to light speed
A perfect physical copy built on arrival
The quantum state, without the particle being sent directly
Only a classical bit with no quantum content

items.explain: Teleportation moves the quantum state of a qubit over a long distance without sending the particle itself.
